neighbours.label: describing how things used to be: the norm of an earlier era, in past tense ('most X were still ...', 'were mostly', 'still used')
fire: In the 1920s, most homes were still heated with coal stoves.
Before the war, telephones were mostly found in offices and shops.
Back then, nearly all letters were still written by hand.
In medieval towns, most streets were unpaved and muddy.
Early on, radios were mostly built by hobbyists at home.
A century ago, most children still walked miles to school.
In those years, sailors still used the stars to find their way.
Around 1900, most bread was baked at home rather than bought.
quiet: Today, most homes are heated with gas or heat pumps.
Nowadays, telephones are carried by almost everyone.
These days, nearly all letters are typed on a computer.
In modern towns, most streets are paved and lit at night.
Now, radios are built in large factories overseas.
Today, most children ride a bus or bike to school.
Modern sailors rely on satellite navigation to find their way.
Most bread today is bought from a shop or supermarket.

notes: Drawn pole is + (card: 'there was only soft or English wheat', 'nurses were mostly referred to', 'most firearms were single shot', 'all nations still used telegraphy'). Probes 0.22-0.35 on still/mostly/used; a present-tense control read 0.06.
